title: V. The Third Ordeal
paragraphs: Mitya spoke sullenly, but it was plain he was working harder than ever not to forget or skip a single detail. He told them how he had jumped the fence into his father’s garden and crept up to the window. He told them everything that happened under that window. Clearly and precisely, step by step, he described what he felt in the garden during those moments, when he was desperate to know whether Grushenka was with his father or not. But, strange to say, both lawyers now listened with a chilling kind of reserve. They watched him coldly and asked few questions. Mitya could read nothing in their faces.
“They’re angry and offended,” he thought. “Well, forget them!”

Then he told how he had finally made up his mind to give his father the “signal” that Grushenka had come, so that the old man would open the window. The lawyers took no notice of the word “signal.” They seemed not to grasp what it meant here, so plainly that Mitya noticed it. He came at last to the moment when he saw his father peering out of the window, felt his hatred flare up, and pulled the pestle from his pocket. There he suddenly stopped, as if on purpose. He sat staring at the wall, aware that their eyes were fixed on him.
“Well?” said the investigating lawyer. “You took out the weapon, and ... what happened next?”
“Next? Why, next I murdered him ... hit him on the head and cracked his skull.... That’s your version, I suppose. That’s it!”
His eyes flashed suddenly. All the anger he had been smothering burst up in his soul with extraordinary violence.
“Our version?” repeated Nikolay Parfenovitch. “Well, and what is yours?”
Mitya lowered his eyes and said nothing for a long time.

“My version, gentlemen? Well, it went like this,” he began softly. “Maybe it was somebody’s tears, or my mother praying to God, or a good angel kissing me just then. I don’t know. But the devil lost. I tore myself away from the window and ran for the fence. My father was frightened. He saw me then, for the first time, and cried out and leapt back from the window. I remember that very well. I ran across the garden to the fence ... and there Grigory grabbed me, while I was sitting on top of it.”
Only now did he raise his eyes and look at his listeners. They seemed to be staring back with perfectly calm attention. A kind of fit of outrage took hold of Mitya.
“Why, you’re laughing at me this very minute, gentlemen!” he broke off.
“What makes you think so?” said Nikolay Parfenovitch.

“You don’t believe a single word, that’s why! Of course I see I’ve reached the vital point. The old man is lying there with his skull broken, and I—after telling you so dramatically how I wanted to kill him and how I snatched up the pestle—I simply run away from the window. A romance! Poetry! As if anyone could take a fellow at his word. Ha ha! You’re scoffers, gentlemen!”
And he swung around on his chair so hard that it creaked.
“And did you notice,” the prosecutor asked suddenly, as though he had not seen Mitya’s agitation, “as you ran from the window, whether the door into the garden was open?”
“No, it wasn’t open.”
“Not open?”
“It was shut. Who could have opened it? Bah, the door! Wait a minute!” He seemed to remember something all at once, and almost with a start he went on:
“Why, did you find the door open?”
“We did. It was open.”
“But who could have opened it, if you didn’t open it yourselves?” cried Mitya, astonished.

“The door stood open. Your father’s murderer went in by that door without a doubt, and when he had done the deed he went out again by the same door,” said the prosecutor slowly, as though chiseling out each word. “That is perfectly clear. The murder was committed inside the room and _not through the window_. We are quite certain of that from our examination, from the position of the body and everything else. There can be no doubt about it.”
Mitya was struck utterly dumb.

“But that’s completely impossible!” he cried, totally at a loss. “I ... I didn’t go in.... I tell you plainly, definitely, that door was shut the whole time I was in the garden and when I ran out of it. I only stood at the window and saw him through the window. That’s all, that’s all.... I remember it down to the last minute. And even if I didn’t, it would make no difference. I know it, because nobody knew the signals except Smerdyakov, myself and the dead man. And he wouldn’t have opened that door to anyone in the world without the signals.”

“Signals? What signals?” asked the prosecutor, with greedy, almost hysterical curiosity. All his reserve and dignity vanished at once. He asked it with a kind of cringing timidity. He smelled an important fact he had known nothing about, and he was already afraid that Mitya might refuse to reveal it.

“So you didn’t know!” Mitya winked at him, with a spiteful, mocking smile. “And what if I won’t tell you? Who else could you learn it from? Nobody knew about the signals but my father, Smerdyakov and me. That’s all. Heaven knew too, but Heaven won’t tell you. Still, it’s an interesting fact. Who knows what you might build on it! Ha ha! Take heart, gentlemen, I’ll tell you. You’ve got some foolish notion in your heads. You don’t know the man you’re dealing with! You’re dealing with a prisoner who testifies against himself, to his own harm! Yes, because I’m a man of honor, and you—are not.”

The prosecutor swallowed this without a murmur. He was shaking with impatience to hear the new fact. Mitya told them everything about the signals Fyodor Pavlovitch had devised for Smerdyakov, in minute and rambling detail. He told them exactly what each tap on the window meant, and drummed the signals out on the table. When Nikolay Parfenovitch suggested that he must have tapped the signal “Grushenka has come” when he knocked for his father, Mitya answered, quite exactly, that yes, he had tapped that one, “Grushenka has come.”
“So now you can go and build your tower,” Mitya broke off, and again turned away from them in contempt.
“So nobody knew the signals except your dead father, you and the valet Smerdyakov? Nobody else?” Nikolay Parfenovitch asked once again.
“That’s right. The valet Smerdyakov, and Heaven. Put down Heaven. That may be useful. Besides, you’ll be needing God yourselves.”
And of course they had already begun to write it down. But as they wrote, the prosecutor said suddenly, as if seizing on a new idea:

“But if Smerdyakov also knew these signals, and you flatly deny any responsibility for your father’s death, might it not have been he who gave the agreed knock, got your father to open the door to him, and then ... committed the crime?”
Mitya turned on him a look of deep irony and fierce hatred. He stared in silence for so long that the prosecutor blinked.

“You’ve caught the fox again,” Mitya said at last. “You’ve got the beast by the tail. Ha ha! I can see through you, Mr. Prosecutor. You thought, of course, that I’d leap at that, grab at your hint, and shout at the top of my voice, ‘Aie! It’s Smerdyakov! He’s the murderer!’ Admit it, that’s what you thought. Admit it, and I’ll go on.”
But the prosecutor admitted nothing. He kept silent and waited.
“You’re wrong. I’m not going to shout, ‘It’s Smerdyakov,’” said Mitya.
“And you don’t even suspect him?”
“Why, do you?”
“He is under suspicion as well.”
Mitya stared at the floor.

“Joking aside,” he said gloomily. “Listen. From the very start, almost from the moment I ran out to you from behind the curtain, I’ve had Smerdyakov in my mind. I’ve been sitting here shouting that I’m innocent, and all the while I’ve been thinking, ‘Smerdyakov!’ I can’t get Smerdyakov out of my head. In fact, I thought of Smerdyakov just now too, but only for a second. Almost at once I thought, ‘No, it isn’t Smerdyakov.’ It’s not his doing, gentlemen.”
“Then is there anyone else you suspect?” Nikolay Parfenovitch asked carefully.
“I don’t know who it can be, whether it’s the hand of Heaven or of Satan, but ... not Smerdyakov,” Mitya jerked out, with finality.
“But what makes you so sure, and so emphatic, that it isn’t he?”

“It’s my conviction—my impression. Smerdyakov is a man of the most abject character, and a coward. He’s not just a coward, he’s all the cowardice in the world walking about on two legs. He has the heart of a chicken. When he talked to me, he was always trembling in case I killed him, though I never lifted a hand against him. He fell at my feet and blubbered. He has kissed these very boots, literally, begging me ‘not to frighten him.’ Do you hear that? ‘Not to frighten him.’ What a thing to say! Why, I offered him money. He’s a whimpering chicken—sickly, epileptic, feeble-minded—a child of eight could thrash him. He has no character worth mentioning. It’s not Smerdyakov, gentlemen. He doesn’t care for money; he wouldn’t take my gifts. Besides, what reason would he have to murder the old man? Why, he’s very likely his son, you know—his natural son. Did you know that?”
“We have heard that tale. But you are your father’s son too, you know, and yet you told everyone yourself that you meant to murder him.”

“That’s a stab! And a nasty, petty one! I’m not afraid! Oh, gentlemen, isn’t it too low of you to say that to my face? It’s low, because I told you that myself. I not only wanted to murder him, I might have done it. And what’s more, I went out of my way to tell you, of my own free will, that I nearly murdered him. But you see, I didn’t murder him. You see, my guardian angel saved me—that’s what you haven’t taken into account. And that’s why it’s so low of you. Because I didn’t kill him, I didn’t kill him! Do you hear me? I did not kill him.”
He was nearly choking. He had not been so shaken at any point in the whole interrogation.
“And what has he told you, gentlemen—Smerdyakov, I mean?” he added suddenly, after a pause. “Am I allowed to ask that?”

“You may ask any question,” the prosecutor answered with icy severity, “any question that concerns the facts of the case, and we are bound, I repeat, to answer every inquiry you make. We found the servant Smerdyakov, the man you ask about, lying unconscious in his bed, in an epileptic fit of extreme severity, which had come back perhaps ten times. The doctor who came with us examined him and told us he may not live through the night.”
“Well, if that’s so, then the devil must have killed him,” broke suddenly from Mitya, as though until that moment he had been asking himself, “Was it Smerdyakov or not?”
“We will return to this later,” Nikolay Parfenovitch decided. “Now, would you care to continue your statement?”

Mitya asked for a rest, and it was courteously granted. After resting, he went on with his story, but he was clearly low in spirits. He was worn out, humiliated and shaken in his very soul. And to make matters worse, the prosecutor seemed to be irritating him on purpose with tiresome interruptions about “trifling points.” Mitya had hardly described how, sitting on the wall, he struck Grigory on the head with the pestle while the old man clung to his left leg, and how he then jumped down to look at him, when the prosecutor stopped him and asked him to describe exactly how he had been sitting on the wall. Mitya was surprised.
“Oh, I was sitting like this, astride, with one leg on one side of the wall and one on the other.”
“And the pestle?”
“I had the pestle in my hand.”
“Not in your pocket? Do you remember that for certain? Was it a hard blow you gave him?”
“It must have been hard. But why do you ask?”
“Would you be so good as to sit on the chair the way you sat on the wall then, and show us how you moved your arm, and in which direction?”
“You’re making fun of me, aren’t you?” asked Mitya, looking at the speaker with haughty scorn. But the man did not flinch.
Mitya whirled around, sat astride his chair, and swung his arm.
“That’s how I hit him! That’s how I knocked him down! What more do you want?”
“Thank you. Might I trouble you now to explain why you jumped down, what your object was, and what you had in mind?”
“Oh, blast it!... I jumped down to get a look at the man I’d hurt ... I couldn’t tell you why!”
“Though you were worked up and running away?”
“Yes, worked up and running away, and I still jumped down.”
“You wanted to help him?”
“Help!... Yes, maybe I did want to help him.... I can’t remember.”
“You can’t remember? So you weren’t altogether aware of what you were doing?”
“Not at all. I remember everything—every detail. I jumped down to look at him, and I wiped his face with my handkerchief.”
“We’ve seen your handkerchief. Were you hoping to bring him round?”
“I don’t know if I hoped that. I only wanted to find out whether he was alive or dead.”
“Ah! You wanted to find out? Well, and what then?”
“I’m no doctor. I couldn’t tell. I ran off thinking I’d killed him. And now he’s recovered.”
“Excellent,” the prosecutor remarked. “Thank you. That’s all I wanted to hear. Please go on.”

Alas! It never crossed Mitya’s mind to tell them, though he remembered it well, that he had gone back out of pity, and that standing over the man lying there he had even spoken a few words of regret: “You’ve come to grief, old man—there’s no help for it. Well, there you must lie.”

The prosecutor could draw only one conclusion: the man had gone back “at such a moment, and in such agitation, simply to find out whether the _only_ witness of his crime was dead; and so he must be a man of great strength, coolness, resolve and foresight, even at such a moment,” ... and so on. The prosecutor was well pleased. “I’ve provoked this nervous fellow with ‘trifles,’ and he’s said more than he meant to.”
Mitya went on, struggling painfully. But this time Nikolay Parfenovitch cut in right away.
“How was it that you ran to the servant, Fedosya Markovna, with your hands so smeared with blood, and, it seems, your face as well?”
“Why, at the time I never noticed the blood at all,” Mitya answered.
“That’s quite likely. It happens sometimes.” The prosecutor exchanged a look with Nikolay Parfenovitch.
“I just didn’t notice. You’re quite right about that, prosecutor,” Mitya agreed all at once.

Next came the story of how Mitya had suddenly resolved to “step aside” and leave the way clear for their happiness. But he could not bring himself to open his heart to them the way he had before and tell them about “the queen of his soul.” He hated talking about her in front of these cold men “who were fastening on him like bugs.” So, in answer to their repeated questions, he spoke briefly and curtly:

“Well, I decided to kill myself. What did I have left to live for? That question stared me in the face. Her first, rightful lover had come back, the man who’d wronged her but had hurried back after five years to offer her his love and make amends by marrying her.... So I knew it was all over for me.... Behind me was disgrace, and that blood—Grigory’s.... What was there to live for? So I went to redeem the pistols I’d pawned, to load them and put a bullet through my head tomorrow.”
“And a grand feast the night before?”

“Yes, a grand feast the night before. Oh, damn it all, gentlemen! Do hurry up and get this over with. I meant to shoot myself not far from here, out beyond the village, and I’d planned to do it at five in the morning. I even had a note in my pocket by then. I wrote it at Perhotin’s while I was loading the pistols. Here’s the letter. Read it! I’m not saying this for your sake,” he added with contempt. He pulled it from his waistcoat pocket and threw it onto the table. The lawyers read it with interest and, as usual, filed it with the papers of the case.
“And it didn’t even occur to you to wash your hands at Perhotin’s? You weren’t afraid of drawing suspicion?”

“What suspicion? Suspicion or none, I’d have galloped straight here just the same and shot myself at five o’clock, and you’d have been too late to do anything. If it weren’t for what happened to my father, you’d have known nothing and wouldn’t have come here at all. Oh, it’s the devil’s doing. The devil murdered father, and it’s thanks to the devil that you found out so fast. How did you get here so quickly? It’s marvelous, it’s a dream!”

“Mr. Perhotin told us that when you came to him, you were holding ... in your bloodstained hands ... your money ... a lot of money ... a bundle of hundred-rouble notes, and that his servant-boy saw it too.”
“That’s true, gentlemen. I remember that’s how it was.”

“Now, there’s one small point that arises. Can you tell us,” Nikolay Parfenovitch began, very gently, “where you got so much money all of a sudden, when the facts and the timing show that you had not been home?”
The prosecutor’s brows drew together at the question being put so bluntly, but he did not interrupt Nikolay Parfenovitch.
“No, I didn’t go home,” Mitya replied, looking perfectly calm but keeping his eyes on the floor.

“Then let me ask again,” Nikolay Parfenovitch went on, as if creeping up on the subject. “Where could you possibly have found such a sum all at once, when, as you admit yourself, at five o’clock that same day you—”

“I needed ten roubles, so I pawned my pistols with Perhotin, and then I went to Madame Hohlakov to borrow three thousand, which she wouldn’t give me, and so on, and all the rest of it,” Mitya cut in sharply. “Yes, gentlemen, I needed money, and then suddenly there were thousands, eh? Do you know, gentlemen, what you’re both afraid of right now? ‘What if he won’t tell us where he got it?’ Well, that’s just how it is. I’m not going to tell you, gentlemen. You’ve guessed right. You’ll never know,” said Mitya, chipping out each word with extraordinary determination. The lawyers were silent for a moment.
“You must understand, Mr. Karamazov, that it’s vitally important for us to know,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch, in a soft, smooth voice.
“I understand. But I still won’t tell you.”

The prosecutor stepped in too. He reminded the prisoner once more that he was free to decline to answer questions if he judged that to be in his interest, and so on. But given the harm he might do himself by his silence, especially in a case as grave as—

“And so on, gentlemen, and so on. Enough! I’ve heard that rigmarole before,” Mitya broke in again. “I can see for myself how important it is, and that this is the crucial point, and I still won’t say.”
“What does it matter to us? It’s not our affair, it’s yours. You’re hurting yourself,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch nervously.

“Look, gentlemen, joking aside”—Mitya raised his eyes and looked at them both steadily—“I had a feeling from the very beginning that we’d clash at this point. But at first, when I started giving my evidence, it was all still far off and hazy; it was all floating about, and I was so naive that I began by assuming we trusted each other. Now I can see for myself that there can be no such trust, because sooner or later we were bound to run into this cursed stumbling-block. And now we’ve run into it! It’s impossible, and that’s the end of it! But I don’t blame you. You can’t believe it all just because I say so. I understand that, of course.”
He sank back into gloomy silence.

“Could you not, while keeping your resolve to say nothing about the main point, at least give us some small hint of what kind of motives are strong enough to make you refuse to answer, at a moment so dangerous for you?”
Mitya gave a sad, almost dreamy smile.

“I’m a lot more good-natured than you think, gentlemen. I’ll tell you why, and I’ll give you that hint, though you don’t deserve it. I won’t speak of it, gentlemen, because it would stain my honor. The answer to the question of where I got the money would bring me far greater disgrace than murdering and robbing my father would, if I had murdered and robbed him. That’s why I can’t tell you. I can’t, for fear of the disgrace. What, gentlemen, are you going to write that down?”
“Yes, we’ll write it down,” lisped Nikolay Parfenovitch.

“You shouldn’t write that down, about ‘disgrace.’ I only told you out of the goodness of my heart. I didn’t have to tell you. I made you a present of it, so to speak, and you pounce on it right away. Oh, well, write—write whatever you like,” he finished, in scornful disgust. “I’m not afraid of you, and I can still look you in the eye.”
“And can you not tell us what sort of disgrace it is?” Nikolay Parfenovitch ventured.
The prosecutor scowled darkly.
“No, no, _c’est fini_, don’t bother. It isn’t worth dirtying one’s hands. I’ve dirtied myself enough on your account already. You’re not worth it—nobody is ... Enough, gentlemen. I’m not going on.”
He said this too firmly to be argued with. Nikolay Parfenovitch did not press him further, but from Ippolit Kirillovitch’s eyes he could see that the prosecutor had not given up hope.
“Could you at least tell us how much money you had in your hands when you walked into Mr. Perhotin’s—how many roubles, exactly?”
“That I can’t tell you.”
“You told Mr. Perhotin, I believe, that you had three thousand from Madame Hohlakov.”
“Maybe I did. Enough, gentlemen. I won’t say how much I had.”
“Then would you be good enough to tell us how you came here, and what you’ve done since you arrived?”
“Oh! You can ask the people here about that. But I’ll tell you, if you like.”

He proceeded to tell it, but we won’t repeat his story. He told it dryly and curtly. About the raptures of his love he said nothing; he only said that he had dropped his plan of shooting himself because of “new factors in the case.” He gave the story without going into reasons or details. And this time the lawyers did not badger him much. It was plain that nothing here was of any essential interest to them.

“We’ll check all that. We’ll return to it when we examine the witnesses, which will, naturally, be done in your presence,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch in conclusion. “And now let me ask you to put on the table everything you have on you, above all any money you still have.”

“My money, gentlemen? Certainly. I understand that’s needed. I’m actually surprised you didn’t ask about it sooner. It’s true I couldn’t have got away anywhere. I’m sitting here in plain sight. But here’s my money—count it—take it. That’s everything, I think.”

He turned out all his pockets; even the small change—two twenty-copeck pieces—he dug out of his waistcoat pocket. They counted the money. It came to eight hundred and thirty-six roubles and forty copecks.
“And is that all?” the investigating lawyer asked.
“Yes.”
“A moment ago you stated in your evidence that you spent three hundred roubles at Plotnikovs’. You gave Perhotin ten, your driver twenty, you lost two hundred here, then....”
Nikolay Parfenovitch went through all of it. Mitya helped him willingly. They recalled every last farthing and put it in the sum. Nikolay Parfenovitch quickly added up the total.
“With these eight hundred, you must have started with about fifteen hundred?”
“I suppose so,” Mitya snapped.
“Why does everyone claim there was much more?”
“Let them claim it.”
“But you claimed it yourself.”
“Yes, I did, too.”

“We’ll compare all this with the evidence of other people we haven’t yet questioned. Don’t worry about your money. It will be properly looked after and will be returned to you at the end of ... what is now beginning ... if it appears, or, so to speak, is proved, that you have an undisputed right to it. Well, and now....”
Nikolay Parfenovitch suddenly stood up and told Mitya firmly that it was his duty and obligation to carry out a minute and thorough search “of your clothes and everything else....”
“By all means, gentlemen. I’ll turn out every pocket, if you like.”
And he really did begin to turn out his pockets.
“You’ll need to take off your clothes as well.”
“What! Undress? Ugh! Damn it! Won’t you search me as I am? Can’t you?”
“It’s quite out of the question, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You must take your clothes off.”
“Have it your way,” Mitya gave in gloomily; “only please, not here, but behind the curtains. Who’s going to search them?”
“Behind the curtains, naturally.”
Nikolay Parfenovitch nodded his assent. His small face had a look of peculiar solemnity.
